chmmc-2020-individual-01.title: Two triangles, two cones
chmmc-2020-individual-01.body:
The third side is $5$ (if $3,4$ are legs) or $\sqrt7$ (if $4$ is the hypotenuse). The hypotenuse of a right triangle is a diameter of the circumscribed circle, so the base radius is $r=\frac52$ or $r=2$.

The slant height is $3$, so the height is $h=\sqrt{9-r^2}$: $\frac{\sqrt{11}}2$ for $r=\frac52$ and $\sqrt5$ for $r=2$. The volumes $\frac13\pi r^2h$ are $\frac{25\sqrt{11}}{24}\pi\approx10.8$ and $\frac{4\sqrt5}{3}\pi\approx9.4$. The minimum is $\frac{4\pi\sqrt5}{3}$, so $m+n+p=4+5+3=12$.

**Answer: 12**

chmmc-2020-individual-02.title: Count pairs, then correct
chmmc-2020-individual-02.body:
Every pair of students is a side of exactly $2$ equilateral triangles (one on each side of the segment), giving $2\binom{900}2=809100$ (pair, triangle) incidences. A triangle with exactly two student vertices is counted once, but a triangle with all three vertices at students is counted $3$ times. There are $\frac{900}3=300$ such triangles. So the number of distinct triangles is $809100-2\cdot300=808500$.

**Answer: 808500**

chmmc-2020-individual-03.title: Two carries are needed
chmmc-2020-individual-03.body:
If $k$ and $k+1$ both have digit sum divisible by $17$, their digit sums differ by a multiple of $17$. Adding $1$ with $c$ carries changes the digit sum by $1-9c$, so $9c-1\equiv0\pmod{17}$, giving $c=2$ in the allowed range. So $k=\overline{abc99}$ with $c\ne9$, $a\ne0$, and digit sum $a+b+c+18\equiv0\pmod{17}$, i.e. $a+b+c=16$.

The largest such $k$ is $97099$ ($a=9,b=7,c=0$) and the smallest is $17899$ ($a=1,b=7,c=8$). The CIT Beavers are $k+1$, so their difference equals $97099-17899=79200$ (confirmed by exhaustive search).

**Answer: 79200**

chmmc-2020-individual-04.title: Expand in n
chmmc-2020-individual-04.body:
For a cubic, Taylor expansion gives $P(y-n)+P(y+n)=2P(y)+P''(y)\,n^2$ (odd powers cancel, and $P''''=0$). The identity $zP(y)=2P(y)+P''(y)n^2$ for all $n$ forces $P''(y)=0$ and $(z-2)P(y)=0$.

$P''(x)=6x-12$, so $y=2$ and $P(y)=P(2)=8-24-10+4=-22$. Since $P(2)\ne0$ we get $z=2$, consistent.

**Answer: $-22$**

chmmc-2020-individual-05.title: Divisor fractions
chmmc-2020-individual-05.body:
Write $n=2^a3^b$ (with $a,b\ge1$ so a multiple of $6$ can exist). A divisor $2^i3^j$ is a multiple of $6$ iff $i\ge1$ and $j\ge1$, so the fraction of such divisors is $\frac{a}{a+1}\cdot\frac b{b+1}=\frac35$. This gives $5ab=3(a+1)(b+1)$, i.e. $2ab-3a-3b-3=0$, i.e. $(2a-3)(2b-3)=15$.

The factorisations of $15$ give $(a,b)=(2,9),(3,4),(4,3),(9,2)$. Then
$$\frac S{36}=\frac{2^23^9}{36}+\frac{2^33^4}{36}+\frac{2^43^3}{36}+\frac{2^93^2}{36}=3^7+18+12+128=2187+158=2345.$$

**Answer: 2345**

chmmc-2020-individual-06.title: Count how many points are on the dark half
chmmc-2020-individual-06.body:
Let $p$ be the number of the points $P_1,\dots,P_4$ on the dark half and $q$ the number of $Q_1,\dots,Q_4$ on the dark half. The pieces are ordered left to right; the pieces entirely dark are the first $\min(p,q)$, the pieces entirely white are the last $4-\max(p,q)$, and all the rest straddle the boundary, so the number of mixed pieces is $5-\min(p,q)-(4-\max(p,q))=|p-q|+1$.

We need $|p-q|=2$. Each point is on the dark half with probability $\frac12$ independently, so $P(p=k)=\binom4k/16$. The pairs $(p,q)=(4,2),(3,1),(2,0),(2,4),(1,3),(0,2)$ give
$$2\cdot\frac{\binom44\binom42+\binom43\binom41+\binom42\binom40}{16^2}=2\cdot\frac{6+16+6}{256}=\frac7{32}.$$
So $m+n=7+32=39$ (a simulation agrees).

**Answer: 39**

chmmc-2020-individual-07.title: The red graph is forced
chmmc-2020-individual-07.body:
Let the other nine points have red degrees $x_1<\dots<x_9$ in $\{0,\dots,9\}$. If $x_9\le8$ then the degrees are $0,1,\dots,8$, whose sum $36$ plus the odd degree of $A$ is odd, contradicting that the degree sum is even. So $x_9=9$, and then no point has red degree $0$, forcing the degrees to be exactly $1,2,\dots,9$ in order.

Peeling off the extreme points one at a time (degree $9$ is joined to everything, so degree $1$ is joined only to it; then degree $8$ is joined to everyone except the degree-$1$ point, so degree $2$ is joined only to the degrees $9,8$; and so on), the graph is unique: with $N=\{A,B_5,\dots,B_9\}$ and $M=\{B_1,\dots,B_4\}$, all pairs inside $N$ are red, none inside $M$ are, and $B_i$ ($i\le4$) is joined to exactly the $i$ highest-degree points $B_9,\dots,B_{10-i}$ in $N$.

Red triangles: $\binom63=20$ inside $N$, plus for $i=2,3,4$ the triangles with $B_i$ and two of its neighbours: $\binom22+\binom32+\binom42=1+3+6=10$. Total $30$ (verified by constructing the graph).

**Answer: 30**

chmmc-2020-individual-08.title: Telescoping arctangents
chmmc-2020-individual-08.body:
For $j\ge1$, $\tan^{-1}(j^2-j+1)=\frac\pi2-\tan^{-1}\frac1{j^2-j+1}$ and, by the tangent subtraction formula, $\tan^{-1}\frac{1}{1+j(j-1)}=\tan^{-1}\frac{j-(j-1)}{1+j(j-1)}=\tan^{-1}j-\tan^{-1}(j-1)$. The $j=0$ term is $\tan^{-1}1=\frac\pi4$. Therefore
$$\sum_{j=0}^{2020}\tan^{-1}(j^2-j+1)=\frac\pi4+\sum_{j=1}^{2020}\left(\frac\pi2-\tan^{-1}j+\tan^{-1}(j-1)\right)=\frac\pi4+1010\pi-\tan^{-1}2020.$$
So $S=\frac\pi4+1010\pi=\frac{4041\pi}4$ and $m+n=4041+4=4045$.

**Answer: 4045**

chmmc-2020-individual-09.title: Restrict the prime factorisation
chmmc-2020-individual-09.body:
If an odd prime $p$ satisfies $p^2\mid n$, then $p\mid\varphi(n)\mid n^5\sigma(n)-2$, but $p\mid n^5\sigma(n)$, so $p\mid2$: impossible. So $n=2^k\cdot(\text{distinct odd primes})$.

Suppose $k\ge2$ and $n$ has $m\ge1$ odd prime factors. Then $v_2(\varphi(n))\ge(k-1)+m\ge2$, so $4\mid n^5\sigma(n)-2$, but $4\mid n$ gives $n^5\sigma(n)-2\equiv2\pmod4$. Contradiction. If $k=1$ and $m\ge2$ then $v_2(\varphi(n))\ge m\ge2$ and again $n^5\sigma(n)-2\equiv2\pmod 4$: impossible.

*Case $n=2p$ ($p$ odd prime):* $\sigma(n)=3(p+1)$ and $\varphi(n)=p-1$. The condition is $p-1\mid32p^5\cdot3(p+1)-2$; modulo $p-1$ this is $32\cdot6-2=190$. So $p-1\mid190=2\cdot5\cdot19$, with $p-1$ even: $p-1\in\{2,10,190\}$ ($38$ gives $39$, not prime), so $p=3,11,191$ and $n=6,22,382$.

*Case $n=2^k$:* $\varphi=2^{k-1}$, $\sigma=2^{k+1}-1$; for $k\ge3$, $4\mid 2^{k-1}$ but the numerator is $\equiv2\pmod4$, so $k\in\{1,2\}$ and indeed $n=2,4$ work.

Sum: $2+4+6+22+382=416$ (confirmed by search over even $n<20000$).

**Answer: 416**

chmmc-2020-individual-10.title: Where the hacked room sits in the path
chmmc-2020-individual-10.body:
Let $a_1=1,a_2,\dots,a_{60}=60$ be the rooms in the order visited on Monday. A hacked teleporter in room $a_i$ ($1\le i\le59$, each with probability $\frac1{59}$) sends the researcher to a uniformly random other room $a_{j}$ ($j\ne i$; the $59$ values of $j'$ give the $59$ other rooms).

- $i=1$: the researcher goes to some $a_j$, $j\ge2$, and then follows the original path to the exit. Never trapped.
- $2\le i\le59$: if $j>i$ the researcher continues along the path and exits. If $j<i$ she returns to a room already visited whose instructions lead back to $a_i$, so she is trapped. This happens with probability $\frac{i-1}{59}$.

Hence $P=\frac1{59}\sum_{i=2}^{59}\frac{i-1}{59}=\frac1{59^2}\cdot\frac{58\cdot59}2=\frac{29}{59}$, so $m+n=88$ (the same formula $\frac{N-2}{2(N-1)}$ was checked by exhaustive enumeration for $N=5,6,7$ rooms).

**Answer: 88**

chmmc-2020-individual-11.title: Cyclotomic polynomial at 1
chmmc-2020-individual-11.body:
Put $A=1$ on the unit circle and $\omega=e^{2\pi i/n}$; the vertices of the $n$-gon are $\omega^j$, and it shares the vertex $\omega^j$ with a $k$-gon through $A$ ($k<n$) exactly when $\frac jn=\frac{i}{k}$, i.e. when $\gcd(j,n)>1$ (take $k=n/d$ for a common divisor $d>1$; note $k\ge3$ is needed). So for $n\ne4$ the points of $\mathcal S_n$ are the primitive $n$-th roots of unity and $\prod|AQ|=\prod_{\gcd(j,n)=1}|1-\omega^j|=|\Phi_n(1)|$.

It is a standard fact that $\Phi_n(1)=p$ if $n=p^m$ is a prime power and $\Phi_n(1)=1$ otherwise (from $1+z+\dots+z^{n-1}=\prod_{d\mid n,d>1}\Phi_d(z)$ evaluated at $z=1$). So the product is $\le2$ iff $n$ is not a prime power, or $n$ is a power of $2$.

For $n=4$ there is no regular $2$-gon, so the square's vertices $\pm i$ and $-1$ are all in $\mathcal S_4$, with product $\sqrt2\cdot2\cdot\sqrt2=4>2$: $n=4$ fails.

Among the $98$ integers $3\le n\le100$, the inequality fails exactly for the prime powers (there are $34$ of them, including $4,8,16,32,64$) except that $8,16,32,64$ do satisfy it. So the count is $98-34+4=68$ (confirmed by direct computation).

**Answer: 68**

chmmc-2020-individual-12.title: Similar triangles
chmmc-2020-individual-12.body:
Let $O_1,O_2$ be the centres. Since $PA\perp PO_1$ and $PB\perp PO_2$, set $\angle O_1PB=\angle O_2PA=\theta$, so $\angle APB=90^\circ-\theta$ and $\angle O_1PO_2=90^\circ+\theta$. The triangles $CPA$, $O_1PO_2$, $BPD$ are similar (equal inscribed/central angles on chord $PQ$), so $\angle CPA=\angle BPD=90^\circ+\theta$, $PC=PB$ and $PD=PA$ (the line $PO_1$ bisects angle $CPB$ and $PO_2$ bisects $DPA$), and $\angle CPD=90^\circ+3\theta$.

Then $\frac{[CPD]}{PA\cdot PB}=\frac{\frac12PC\cdot PD\sin\angle CPD}{PA\cdot PB}=\frac12\sin(90^\circ+3\theta)=\frac14$, so $\sin(90^\circ+3\theta)=\frac12$, which gives $90^\circ+3\theta\in\{150^\circ,210^\circ,330^\circ\}$ and $\theta\in\{20^\circ,40^\circ,80^\circ\}$ (with $0<\theta<90^\circ$ and $\angle CPD>\angle APB$ meaning $\theta>0$).

So $\angle APB=90^\circ-\theta\in\{70^\circ,50^\circ,10^\circ\}$, with sum $130^\circ$. A numerical construction of the configuration confirms exactly these three values satisfy all conditions.

**Answer: 130**

chmmc-2020-individual-13.title: Symmetric functions
chmmc-2020-individual-13.body:
Let $x=a-b$, $y=b-c$, $z=c-d$ (all $\ge0$) and $p=x+y+z=a-d$, $q=xy+yz+zx$, $r=xyz$. Since $d-a=-p$ the equation becomes
$$x^3+y^3+z^3+2p^3+12\big(p^2-x^2-y^2-z^2\big)+2020\,p\,r=1536.$$
Using $x^3+y^3+z^3=p^3-3pq+3r$ and $p^2-\sum x^2=2q$:
$$3p^3+(24-3p)q+(3+2020p)\,r=1536.$$
Suppose $p>8$. Then $24-3p<0$ and $q\le\frac{p^2}3$, so the left side is at least $3p^3+(24-3p)\frac{p^2}3+0=2p^3+8p^2>2\cdot512+8\cdot64=1536$: impossible. So $p\le8$.

$p=8$ is attained: take $z=0$ so $r=0$; the left side is $3\cdot512+(24-24)q=1536$. Hence $a-d\le8$ and the minimum of $d-a$ is $-8$.

**Answer: $-8$**

chmmc-2020-individual-14.title: Two circles through P and Q
chmmc-2020-individual-14.body:
Let $F=(0,a)$ and $G=(0,-a)$ and $R$ a point with $RF^2=x^2+(y-a)^2$, $RG^2=x^2+(y+a)^2$. By the law of cosines, $FG^2=4a^2=RF^2+RG^2-2RF\cdot RG\cos\angle FRG$. The first equation says $\cos\angle FRG=\frac12$, i.e. $\angle FRG=60^\circ$, and the second says $\angle FRG=120^\circ$. These loci are arcs of two circles $\omega_1,\omega_2$ of radius $r=\frac{2a}{\sqrt3}$ through $F,G$ whose centres are at distance $r$ from each other (each passes through the other's centre).

Following the official solution, let $Z_1,Z_3\in\omega_1$ and $Z_2,Z_4\in\omega_2$. The chords $Z_1Z_3=6$ and $Z_2Z_4=4$ have midpoints $4$ apart along the line, and the centres are at distances $\sqrt{r^2-9}$ and $\sqrt{r^2-4}$ from the line, so (right trapezoid)
$$4^2+\left(\sqrt{r^2-4}-\sqrt{r^2-9}\right)^2=r^2\ \Longrightarrow\ r^2=\frac{29+2\sqrt{109}}3,$$
(the other root makes the square roots non-real). Then $a^2=\frac34r^2=\frac{29+2\sqrt{109}}4$ and $m+n+p+q=29+2+109+4=144$.

**Answer: 144**

chmmc-2020-individual-14.title: Another arrangement
chmmc-2020-individual-14.body: A numerical search shows the conditions can also be met with $Z_1,Z_4\in\omega_1$ and $Z_2,Z_3\in\omega_2$. Then the chords are $Z_1Z_4=9$ and $Z_2Z_3=1$ with midpoints $1$ apart, and the same trapezoid argument gives $r^2=\frac{42+7\sqrt{129}}6$, so $a^2=\frac{42+7\sqrt{129}}8$ and $m+n+p+q=42+7+129+8=186$. The official answer uses only the first arrangement.

chmmc-2020-individual-15.title: Hall's theorem
chmmc-2020-individual-15.body:
Quasi-perfect means $K$ is larger than a permutation matrix and contains one. By Hall's theorem a quasi-complete $H$ has no permutation matrix iff some set of $i$ rows ($2\le i\le n-1$) has at most $i-1$ columns of $H$-cells among them. Such an $H$ has at most $i(i-1)+n(n-i)$ cells (a block of $i$ rows using $i-1$ columns, plus the other $n-i$ rows full); this is convex in $i$ so it is at most $n^2-2n+2$, attained at $i=2$ and $i=n-1$.

So an $H$ with $n^2-2n+3$ cells always has a permutation matrix (and is larger than it): $\vartheta(n)\le n^2-2n+3$, and the example "first $n-2$ columns full plus one cell in each of the last two columns, in the same row" shows quasi-complete non-quasi-perfect sets of size $n^2-2n+2$ exist, so $\vartheta(n)=n^2-2n+3$.

The extremal non-quasi-perfect sets of size $n^2-2n+2$ are of two types: two rows containing a single cell each, both in the same column, all other rows full ($\binom n2\cdot n$ sets), and the transposed type ($\binom n2\cdot n$ sets). For $n\ge4$ these are distinct, so $\varrho(n)=n^2(n-1)$ (brute force: $\varrho(4)=48$, $\vartheta(4)=11$).

For $n=20$: $\vartheta(20)=363$, $\varrho(20)=400\cdot19=7600$, total $7963$.

**Answer: 7963**
